content.content: WHEN focus moves onto a node by a means other than a pointer click on that node, the viewer shall centre the viewport on that node, leaving the zoom level unchanged. WHEN an id the detail panel lists in one of its four relationship sections is activated, the viewer shall centre the viewport on the node that activation selects, leaving the zoom level unchanged: what an activation is, and which node it selects, are kwxutvpw's to settle, and this rule takes both from it and adds only this consequence for the viewport. Either trigger produces a centring move, and the node a centring move centres on is the node its trigger identifies - the node focus moved onto, or the node the activation selected. The trigger is stated for activation on its own rather than left to the first, so that no centring depends on whether an activation moves focus; where a move answers to both triggers, it is one and the same move. On an axis where the graph fits within the viewport, a centring move shall bring the centre of the node it centres on to the viewport centre, and margin on that axis is permitted: the pan limits this viewer records do not hold a centring move back there. On an axis where the graph overflows the viewport, the graph shall keep covering the viewport, and the pan limits this viewer records shall bind that axis: a centring move is not carried past those limits there. This rule governs a centring move alone; the clamp this viewer records for a pan or a zoom is left as it is recorded. WHEN the user clicks a node's own box in the graph with a pointer, the viewer shall not move the viewport: that click is the selection gesture ltrnmrsr records, and it centres nothing. The click carved out here is the click on a node's own box; a pointer click on a listed id in one of the panel's four relationship sections is a different gesture on a different surface - it is an activation (kwxutvpw), and so it falls under the trigger above and starts the same centring move. Neither rule reaches a change of the panel's own focus, and an activation is not such a change: focus arriving on a listed entry is a change of the panel's own focus and moves nothing, while what the second trigger reaches is the activation, which is the selection kwxutvpw settles and not a change of the panel's focus. Nor does either rule reach a focus that ends with no node focused as when a graph reload removes the focused node; those shall not move the viewport. Centring is a viewport move and nothing else: keyboard traversal order and its wrap, the visible focus emphasis on the focused node, the zoom that keeps its rule of zooming about the viewport centre, and the selection and detail a click or an activation produces all remain as their own decisions set them.
content.rationale:
A focus move is not the only way a node comes to be named from somewhere the reader is not looking. Keyboard traversal forwards and backwards (ruqsmuxz, rwonulnq) can carry focus to a node that is off screen, and the detail panel lists the ids of the selected node's relationships (rmovtvkt), which kwxutvpw makes entries that select the node each id names; activating an entry therefore puts the reader on a node whose box may be anywhere in the graph, off screen as easily as the node a Tab press lands on. Centring on that node is the same move the first trigger makes, and it is the same move for the same reason: what the reader has just chosen is a node, and the useful thing to do with a node chosen by name is to show where it is. The trigger is added to this rule's trigger set instead of being given a rule of its own, which is also why the axis and limit terms needed nothing new - a fitted axis still brings the node's centre to the viewport centre with the margin accepted, an overflowing axis still keeps the graph covering the viewport with the recorded limits binding, and the zoom level is still left alone, because a centring move is a centring move however the node is named. Which node the move centres on is whichever node its trigger identifies, so the axis terms speak of the node the move centres on rather than of the focused node alone; nothing else in those terms changed.

Which node an activation selects is not this rule's to settle, and it is not restated here. kwxutvpw settles what an activation is and that the entry's id decides the selected node; this node cites it for both and states the consequence for the viewport, nothing more. A second copy of that definition in this node would be a second thing to keep true, and it would fail exactly where two copies can: a reworded activation upstream would leave this copy silently disagreeing with it, and a reader could not tell which one governed. The citation is load-bearing rather than decorative - the trigger is that activation as it stands, so if an id that names no node document stays inert (rusopkql) or the inputs of an activation are otherwise fixed, the trigger narrows and widens with kwxutvpw while no wording here needs to change. The trigger is also stated directly for activation rather than read off the first trigger's 'a means other than a pointer click on that node', because whether an activation moves focus belongs to kwxutvpw and ltrnmrsr and not to this rule: centring must not hinge on an assumption about focus this node has no licence to make, and where an activation does also carry focus onto the node, both triggers identify the same node and the same move.

Centring is neither a pan nor a zoom - a pan is what a drag does (srsnqppq) and a zoom is what a scroll or pinch does (kyokxuml) - so the clamp yymrxqsk records does not reach a centring move on its own terms, and the rule therefore settles for itself where, and on what condition, a recorded limit reaches one. The axis decides that condition, because the covering the limits protect is achievable on one kind of axis and not the other. On an axis where the graph fits inside the viewport, no pan of any extent can make the graph cover that axis, so holding a centring move back would surrender the whole point of centring - the node the move centres on landing where the eye already is - in exchange for a covering that is unattainable; there the node's centre goes to the viewport centre and the margin left at the edge is accepted. On an axis where the graph overflows the viewport the covering is attainable and the recorded limits already say where the graph may stop, so a recorded limit binds a centring move there and the move is not carried past it: that is why the carve-out is drawn per axis rather than per move, and why centring on an overflowing axis gains no freedom this decision gives it. The rule adds nothing to those limits elsewhere: a pan and a zoom keep the clamp yymrxqsk records, on the same trigger and to the same extent, since centring neither excepts nor re-routes them.

The pointer carve-out is kept for the gesture it was drawn for, and the arrival of the second trigger is what makes the distinction worth stating. ltrnmrsr makes a click on a node's box the selection gesture, and this rule keeps that click from moving the viewport, exactly as recorded; a pointer click on a listed id in the panel is a different gesture on a different surface - it is an activation, kwxutvpw's trigger, whose outcome is the selection of the node the entry names - and it is the very move the second trigger puts a centring move behind. So the two sentences do not collide: the node's own box is the surface whose click centres nothing, the listed entry is the surface whose click activates and therefore centres, and neither sentence is read as qualifying the other. Nothing here re-decides ltrnmrsr or kwxutvpw: a box click still selects and shows detail, an activation still selects the node its id names, and the only thing this node adds is where the viewport stands when an activation, rather than a box click, does the selecting.

The boundary at pltovtuo is deliberate and is kept. A change in the panel's own focus is not focus arriving at a node, and a focus that ends with nothing focused, as when a reload removes the focused node, is not focus moving onto a node either - both keep pan, zoom and selection exactly as that decision holds them. An activation does not fall on the wrong side of that boundary: focus arriving on a listed entry, which is the focus the keyboard input needs, is a change of the panel's own focus and moves nothing, while what this trigger reaches is the activation, which is the selection kwxutvpw settles and not a change of the panel's own focus. Reading the entry and invoking it are thus separated at the same line pltovtuo drew: a reader who tabs onto an entry and stops there moves no viewport, and a reader who invokes it gets the selection kwxutvpw fixes and the centring this node adds, so no panel focus change is handed a viewport move it did not already have. The reload case keeps its place for the same reason: a focus that ends with no node focused names no node, whereas an activation always selects a node the panel already has and cannot end with nothing selected.

Centring is a viewport move only: it does not reorder or skip any step of traversal or its wrap (ruqsmuxz, rwonulnq), it does not change how the focus emphasis ozxnxzus specifies is shown, it does not rescale anything and so leaves pposortu's zoom about the viewport centre governing every zoom, and it does not change the selection or the detail an activation produces or the detail a click produces (ltrnmrsr), so each of those stays in force with nothing overridden.
